# Outline

## Introduction

Opens by framing the gap between homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysis in biological-inspired systems. Introduces metal-organic frameworks as structural mimics of enzyme active sites, arguing that spatial confinement of H2O and CO2 binding events is the key missing design principle. Closes with the perspective thesis: that explicit active-site mimicry unlocks selectivity regimes inaccessible to conventional porous materials.

## Results

Presents kinetic and structural evidence for the two-step gating mechanism. Ca2+ coordination data across pH gradient are the centrepiece. Temperature-dependent Arrhenius analysis quantifies the conformational penalty. Heterologous expression in E. coli benchmarks biological relevance.

## Discussion

Reconciles the new mechanistic picture with apparently contradictory prior literature. Emphasises framework flexibility as the overlooked variable. Connects CO2 fixation efficiency to pore chemistry metrics that can be tuned synthetically.

## Conclusion

Distils the perspective into two actionable design rules and points toward the next experimental step.
